Question ten. How would you estimate the size of something on the spot? Break it into factors, and say every assumption out loud. Daily searches for a new search-by-ingredient feature: two million monthly users, a quarter of them use it, half a session a day each, two searches a session. About five hundred thousand a day. The interviewer is grading the structure and the sanity check, not the number. Question eleven. How do you size a feature's impact before building it? Bound it. A hundred and twenty thousand weekly users reach the screen it lives on. Similar launches lifted cooking one to three percent. That's twelve hundred to thirty-six hundred extra weekly cooks, against a goal of twenty thousand. Even the best case is under a fifth of it. The cheapest experiment is the arithmetic.

Three left, each about a number you already have. When two metrics pull apart, name which is the goal and which is the limit. A notification change that lifts sessions five percent but raises unsubscribes two is only a win if the long-run math nets out positive. A vanity metric looks good and only goes up, like total signups. Ask: if it doubled, would you know what to do differently? Prefer rates and cohorts, like week-four retention. And a ratio can move because of its top, its bottom, or the mix underneath. Saves per user rose from two to two point four while saves fell, because a fifth of the users left. Read both halves, and add up counts across groups rather than averaging their ratios. Every case in this round ends with someone pulling the numbers. In the next one, that's you, in Python. Next: Python and pandas.
